content: As with any surgical procedure, a cesarean section carries both shortand long-term risks. These risks can persist for many years after the delivery and may impact the health of the mother, the child, and future pregnancies. In the short term, cesarean sections are associated with an increased likelihood of requiring a blood transfusion, complications related to anesthesia, organ injury, infection, thromboembolic disease, and neonatal respiratory distress, among other complications. In the long term, cesarean sections have been linked to a higher risk of asthma and obesity in children, as well as complications in subsequent pregnancies. These complications include uterine rupture, placenta accreta, placenta previa, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, hysterectomy, and intra-abdominal adhesions. The risk of these complications increases progressively with the number of prior cesarean deliveries. The global rate of cesarean sections has been steadily rising over the past few decades, often exceeding levels that are medically necessary. This trend has not been accompanied by significant improvements in maternal or perinatal outcomes. While cesarean sections can be life-saving for both the mother and baby when performed for medical reasons, unnecessary cesarean deliveries pose avoidable risks. To address this issue, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends several non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. These include educational programs for women, such as childbirth training workshops, relaxation training, psychosocial couple-based prevention programs, and psychoeducation for women with anxiety or fear of pain. Additionally, the use of evidence-based clinical guidelines, audits, and feedback for healthcare professionals is encouraged. Insurance reforms, such as equalizing physician fees for vaginal and cesarean births, may also be considered in the context of rigorous research. The WHO emphasizes the importance of understanding the local context when implementing interventions to reduce cesarean rates. Factors such as maternal obesity, higher maternal age, an increase in multiple births, and a greater proportion of first-time mothers have been cited as contributors to the rise in cesarean rates. Non-clinical factors, including fear of pain, fear of litigation, organizational practices, financial incentives, and socio-cultural norms, also play a role. Addressing these factors is crucial to reducing unnecessary cesarean sections. The WHO recommends the Robson Classification System as a global standard for monitoring and assessing cesarean section rates and maternal and perinatal outcomes. This system takes into account the specific characteristics of the populations served, such as obstetric case mix. It is essential to integrate these recommendations with broader WHO guidelines on intrapartum and antenatal care to improve the quality of care and achieve optimal health outcomes for mothers and babies.
